title: Later Wittgenstein and Ordinary Language
subtitle: The philosopher who tore up his own masterpiece and found meaning in the market square
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain why the later Wittgenstein rejected the picture theory of his own Tractatus.
By the end you will be able to describe language games, meaning as use and family resemblance with everyday examples.
By the end you will be able to summarise the private language argument and the beetle-in-the-box image.
By the end you will be able to explain J.L. Austin's idea that saying something can be doing something.
By the end you will be able to judge what ordinary language philosophy got right and where critics think it went wrong.
hook:
Try to define the word *game*. Chess is a game, but so is ring-a-ring-a-roses, and so are poker, football, solitaire and the Olympic Games. Is it competition? Solitaire has no opponent. Winning and losing? A child throwing a ball against a wall has no winner. Rules? Make-believe has hardly any. Fun? Professional chess at the highest level is often agony. Every definition you try either lets in things that are not games or shuts out things that obviously are.

And yet you use the word perfectly well. You have never once been confused about whether to call tag a game. This little puzzle became the starting point for one of the strangest turns in the history of philosophy. On Day 70 you met the young Ludwig Wittgenstein, who believed he had solved all the problems of philosophy in the *Tractatus*. Today you meet the older Wittgenstein, who decided he had been profoundly wrong, and who taught a generation of philosophers to stop looking for hidden essences and start looking at how words are actually used.

sections.heading: The Return of the Exile
sections.body:
After finishing the *Tractatus* (published 1921), Wittgenstein did something that only he would do: having solved philosophy, he left it. He gave away his share of one of the largest fortunes in Austria, worked as a schoolteacher in remote mountain villages, served as a gardener's assistant at a monastery, and helped design a severe, beautiful house for his sister in Vienna.

But doubts crept in. Conversations with members of the Vienna Circle (Day 71), who admired the *Tractatus* more than he did, and with the economist Piero Sraffa and the philosopher Frank Ramsey in Cambridge, convinced him that something was badly wrong with his earlier picture. In 1929 he returned to Cambridge. He submitted the *Tractatus* as his doctoral thesis; the examiners were Bertrand Russell and G.E. Moore, and Moore's report is said to have called it a work of genius that in any case met the standard for a PhD.

Wittgenstein taught at Cambridge on and off until 1947, in famously intense sessions in his bare rooms, pacing, falling silent, cursing his own stupidity. He published almost nothing more in his lifetime. His second great book, the ***Philosophical Investigations***, appeared in 1953, two years after his death from cancer in 1951. Its style could not be more different from the *Tractatus*. Instead of numbered pronouncements carved like a legal code, it is a long chain of remarks, questions, imagined objections and little scenes, as if we are overhearing a philosopher argue with himself. He wrote in the preface that he had been forced to recognise grave mistakes in his first book.

sections.heading: Language Games: Words as Tools
sections.body:
The *Investigations* opens by quoting Augustine (Day 30), who remembered learning language as a child by watching adults point at objects and say their names. Wittgenstein says this captures a particular picture: every word names an object, and the object is its meaning. That was more or less the picture behind the *Tractatus* too, where sentences mirror facts.

Wittgenstein then imagines a very simple language. A builder and his assistant use only four words: *block*, *pillar*, *slab* and *beam*. When the builder calls out a word, the assistant brings the matching stone. Notice, he says, that *slab!* here is not really a name for a slab. It works more like an order: bring me a slab. Its meaning lies in the role it plays in the activity.

He calls activities like this **language games**: patterns of speaking woven together with patterns of doing. Giving orders, describing an object, reporting an event, making up a story, telling a joke, thanking, cursing, greeting, praying. Each has its own rules, and the same words can do different jobs in different games. Think of how *fine* works in “I'm fine,” “That's a fine mess,” and “You'll pay a fine.” He compares words to the tools in a toolbox: hammer, pliers, saw, screwdriver, glue. We are misled because words *look* alike on the page, just as the handles in a locomotive cab look alike though one is a crank, one a switch, one a brake.

From this comes his most famous slogan, **meaning as use**: for a large class of cases, he says, the meaning of a word is its use in the language. To understand a word is not to have a picture in your head or to grasp an invisible essence. It is to know how to go on with it: to use it correctly, respond to it appropriately, and take part in the practices it belongs to. Language, for the later Wittgenstein, is part of a **form of life**, the shared background of human activities, interests and reactions that makes speech possible. That is why he could write that if a lion could talk, we could not understand it: we would not share its form of life.

sections.heading: Family Resemblance: Don't Think, Look!
sections.body:
Now return to the puzzle about games. Wittgenstein's advice is blunt: don't say there *must* be something common to all games, or they would not be called games. Instead, look and see. When you do, you find a complicated network of similarities, overlapping and criss-crossing. Board games share some features with card games, card games share others with ball games, and some of those disappear in ring-a-ring-a-roses.

He calls this **family resemblance**. In a family, one person has the grandfather's nose, another his eyes and the mother's walk, a third the mother's walk and an aunt's laugh. There need be no single feature that every family member has, yet the resemblance is real. He also uses the image of a thread: its strength does not come from one fibre running the whole length, but from many fibres overlapping.

This was a quiet bomb dropped on a habit as old as Socrates. Remember how Socrates on Day 9 demanded the single definition of courage or piety, and dismissed lists of examples as beside the point? And Plato's Forms (Day 11) were the ultimate essences behind each general word. Wittgenstein suggests that for many of our concepts there is no such essence to find. That does not make the concepts vague or useless. We can draw sharper boundaries for special purposes, as a referee or a dictionary does, but the concept works perfectly well without them.

Think about how much philosophical energy has gone into finding the essence of *art*, *religion*, *knowledge* or *life*. If Wittgenstein is right, at least some of these quests were doomed from the start, not because the questions are too hard but because they assume something that is not there.

sections.heading: The Private Language Argument and the Beetle in the Box
sections.body:
One of the most debated passages in the *Investigations* (roughly sections 243 to 315) asks whether there could be a **private language**: a language whose words refer to the speaker's inner sensations and that, in principle, nobody else could understand. Descartes (Day 43) seemed to assume something like this. I know my own mind directly, from the inside; my word *pain* gets its meaning from my private experience.

Wittgenstein imagines someone keeping a diary. Each time he has a certain sensation, he writes the sign *S*. How does he know he is using *S* correctly the next time? He can only check against his memory of the sensation. But then, Wittgenstein says, whatever is going to seem right to him is right, and that only means we cannot talk about right at all. A rule you cannot possibly get wrong is not a rule. Meaning requires public criteria for correct use, something that could in principle be checked.

His most memorable image is the **beetle in the box**. Suppose everyone has a box with something in it that they call a beetle. Nobody can look into anyone else's box; each knows what a beetle is only by looking at their own. It could be that everyone has something different, or that the thing keeps changing, or even that a box is empty. Yet the word *beetle* is used in a perfectly ordinary way. Conclusion: the thing in the box drops out of the language game altogether. Whatever gives *beetle* its meaning, it is not the private object.

Wittgenstein is *not* saying that sensations do not exist, though critics have often read him as a behaviourist. His point is about how sensation words get their meaning: through their place in shared life, in crying, wincing, comforting and reporting. A child learns *it hurts* as a replacement for crying, not by inner labelling. Scholars still disagree about exactly what the argument proves. Saul Kripke's 1982 reading linked it to a deeper puzzle about following any rule at all, a reading many Wittgenstein specialists reject as more Kripke than Wittgenstein.

sections.heading: Philosophy as Therapy
sections.body:
Why does any of this matter? Because Wittgenstein thought the great traditional problems of philosophy arise when language goes on holiday: when we take words out of the games where they work and ask questions in a vacuum. We ask *what is time?* and feel baffled, though we never struggle to say *see you at four*. Augustine had exactly this experience (Day 31): he knew what time was until someone asked him.

So philosophy, he wrote, is a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by means of language. Its job is not to build theories or discover hidden facts but to assemble reminders of how we actually speak, so that the puzzle dissolves. In one famous line he asks what his aim in philosophy is, and answers: to show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle. The fly keeps banging against the glass; it does not need a new theory of glass, it needs to see the opening it came in through.

This **therapeutic** view of philosophy is beautiful and also deeply controversial. Many philosophers felt it threatened to dissolve real questions about mind, ethics and knowledge into word games. Bertrand Russell, his old mentor, came to dislike the later work intensely; he complained that it seemed to abandon serious thinking, and mocked the ordinary language philosophy it inspired as a study of the different ways in which silly people can say silly things. Others found it liberating. Either way, notice the continuity with the young Wittgenstein: both books treat philosophy as an activity of clarification rather than a body of doctrine.

sections.heading: Oxford and Ordinary Language: Ryle and Austin
sections.body:
In the 1940s and 1950s a related movement flourished at Oxford, usually called **ordinary language philosophy**. Its members shared the conviction that careful attention to how words are really used can expose philosophical confusion.

Gilbert Ryle's *The Concept of Mind* (1949) attacked what he called the dogma of the **ghost in the machine**, Descartes' picture of an immaterial mind steering a mechanical body. Ryle diagnosed it as a **category mistake**. Imagine a visitor shown Oxford's colleges, libraries and laboratories who then asks: but where is the University? He has mistaken the University for one more building, when it is the way all of these are organised. Similarly, Ryle argued, the mind is not an extra thing inside the body but a matter of how a person behaves and is disposed to behave.

J.L. Austin (1911–1960) was the movement's most meticulous practitioner. He ran Saturday morning discussions where colleagues would spend weeks on the difference between doing something *by mistake* and *by accident*. (Austin's own example: you shoot your neighbour's donkey thinking it is yours; that is a mistake. You aim at your donkey, but it moves and you hit his; that is an accident.)

Austin's lasting contribution came in lectures given at Harvard in 1955 and published as *How to Do Things with Words* (1962). Philosophers had assumed that sentences mainly describe things and are true or false. But consider: “I do” (at a wedding), “I name this ship the *Queen Elizabeth*,” “I bet you five pounds it will rain,” “I promise.” These do not describe an action; saying them, in the right circumstances, *is* the action. Austin called them **performatives**, and the whole approach the study of **speech acts**.

Performatives are not true or false, but they can go wrong: they can be infelicitous. If a random passer-by says “I now pronounce you married,” nothing happens. Austin listed **felicity conditions**: the right person, the right procedure, the right circumstances, sincerity. He then distinguished the *locutionary* act (saying words with a meaning), the *illocutionary* act (what you do in saying them: warning, promising, ordering) and the *perlocutionary* act (what you bring about by saying them: frightening, persuading). “The ice is thin” can be a warning, and can succeed in scaring someone off. His student John Searle developed this into a full theory, and you will meet a famous quarrel between Searle and Derrida about Austin on Day 81.

Critics, notably Bertrand Russell and Ernest Gellner in his scathing *Words and Things* (1959), accused ordinary language philosophy of conservatism and triviality: why should the way people happen to talk settle anything? Austin's reply was modest: ordinary language is not the last word, but it is the first word, a storehouse of distinctions that generations found worth making.

keyQuote.text: For a large class of cases—though not for all—in which we employ the word “meaning” it can be defined thus: the meaning of a word is its use in the language.
keyQuote.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations, §43 (trans. G.E.M. Anscombe)

modernConnection.title: Chatbots and the Company Words Keep
modernConnection.body:
Today's large language models, the systems behind AI chatbots, are a strange real-world test of Wittgenstein's slogan. They are not programmed with definitions or with links between words and objects. They are trained on enormous amounts of text and learn, statistically, how each word tends to be used: which words surround it, what follows it, what contexts it appears in. Linguists call this *distributional semantics*, and its motto, from the English linguist J.R. Firth in 1957, sounds like a footnote to the *Investigations*: you shall know a word by the company it keeps.

The success of these systems is in one way a vindication of meaning as use. A model that has never seen a game can still sort out *game* in “a game of chess,” “game for anything” and “big game hunting” purely from patterns of use. It handles family-resemblance concepts with no essential definitions at all.

But here the comparison gets interesting, and honest about its limits. For Wittgenstein, use was never just patterns of words. Language games are woven into a form of life: building, promising, comforting someone in pain, being held to account. A model learns the textual traces of those activities, not the activities themselves. Does it *understand*, or does it imitate the surface of understanding? Wittgensteinians split on this. Some say that if use is meaning, competent use is all there is to understanding. Others say the model plays word-patterns without ever playing the game, like someone who knows every move in chess notation but has never wanted to win.

Austin's speech acts raise a parallel puzzle. When a chatbot says “I promise to be more careful,” has a promise been made? Felicity conditions require sincerity and the ability to be held to the commitment. You will return to these questions with the Chinese Room on Day 84 and AI ethics on Day 89.

vocabulary.definition: Wittgenstein's term for an activity in which speaking is woven together with doing, governed by its own implicit rules.
vocabulary.example: Ordering a coffee, telling a bedtime story and swearing an oath are different language games, even if some of the same words appear in each.

vocabulary.definition: The view that, in many cases, a word's meaning is not an object it names or an image in the mind but the role it plays in the practices of a language.
vocabulary.example: Knowing the meaning of *checkmate* is knowing how it is used in chess, not having a mental picture of it.

vocabulary.definition: A network of overlapping similarities among things grouped under one concept, with no single feature shared by all of them.
vocabulary.example: Sports form a family resemblance: some use balls, some are timed, some are scored by judges, but no one feature unites them all.

vocabulary.definition: The shared background of human activities, needs and natural reactions within which language games make sense.
vocabulary.example: Wittgenstein said that if a lion could talk we could not understand it, because we do not share its form of life.

vocabulary.definition: A hypothetical language whose words refer to experiences that only the speaker could know, which Wittgenstein argued is impossible because meaning requires public criteria of correctness.
vocabulary.example: The diary in which someone writes *S* for a sensation nobody else can check is Wittgenstein's test case for a private language.

vocabulary.definition: Gilbert Ryle's name for treating something as belonging to the wrong logical type, such as treating the mind as an extra ghostly object.
vocabulary.example: Asking to see the University after touring all its colleges and libraries is a category mistake.

vocabulary.definition: J.L. Austin's term for an utterance that does not describe an action but performs it, given the right circumstances.
vocabulary.example: When the judge says “I sentence you to five years,” she is not reporting a sentence; she is passing it.

vocabulary.definition: An action performed by means of an utterance, such as promising, warning, ordering or apologising.
vocabulary.example: “Watch out, the floor is wet” is grammatically a description but its main speech act is a warning.

thinkingExercise.title: Hunt for an Essence
thinkingExercise.prompt: Test Wittgenstein's family-resemblance idea on a concept you care about, and see whether a Socratic definition survives.
steps: Pick one concept: *art*, *friendship*, *religion*, *sport* or *work*. Write down ten varied examples of it, including some borderline ones.
Try to write a one-sentence definition that covers all ten and excludes obvious non-examples. Note every counterexample that breaks it.
Now draw the family resemblance instead: list four or five features and mark which examples have which. Is there any feature that every example shares?
Choose one sentence using your concept and describe two different language games in which it could be used to do different things (for example, praising versus ruling something out).
Write a short paragraph: did your concept turn out to have an essence after all, or did Wittgenstein's view fit better? What would Socrates say back?

summary: The later Wittgenstein rejected his own *Tractatus* picture in which words name objects and sentences mirror facts.
In the *Philosophical Investigations* (1953) he argued that language is a collection of language games embedded in forms of life, and that meaning is often best understood as use.
Many concepts, like *game*, are held together by family resemblance rather than a single shared essence, challenging the Socratic search for definitions.
The private language argument and the beetle in the box suggest that sensation words get their meaning from public practices, not inner objects.

Oxford ordinary language philosophy, especially Ryle's category mistake and Austin's speech acts, used close attention to everyday speech to dissolve philosophical confusion, though critics charged it with triviality and conservatism.

quiz.question: What is the main idea behind Wittgenstein's builders who use the words block, pillar, slab and beam?
options: That every word is a name for a physical object
That simple languages are logically superior to complex ones
That a word's meaning comes from the role it plays in an activity
That language must be learned through formal definitions
quiz.explanation: The builders show that *slab!* functions more like an order within an activity than as a mere label, illustrating meaning as use. The point is precisely to challenge the idea that words simply name objects.

quiz.question: According to Wittgenstein, why can't we find a single definition of *game*?
options: Because games are held together by overlapping similarities rather than one common feature
Because the word is too new to have settled
Because only experts can define games
Because games are private experiences
quiz.explanation: Family resemblance means a network of criss-crossing similarities, like the faces of a family, with no essence shared by all.

quiz.question: The *Philosophical Investigations* was published during Wittgenstein's lifetime as his doctoral thesis.
quiz.explanation: It was published in 1953, two years after his death. His doctoral thesis, submitted in 1929, was the *Tractatus*.

quiz.question: What is the conclusion of the beetle-in-the-box image?
options: Everyone's private experiences are identical
We can never use words for sensations at all
Sensations do not exist
The private object drops out of the language game; it is not what gives the word its meaning
quiz.explanation: Since no one can check anyone else's box, whatever is inside plays no role in the public use of *beetle*. Wittgenstein is not denying that sensations exist.

quiz.question: Which of these is a performative utterance in Austin's sense?
options: “The cat is on the mat.”
“I bet you ten dollars the train is late.”
“Paris is the capital of France.”
“It rained yesterday.”
quiz.explanation: Saying “I bet you…” in the right circumstances is making the bet, not describing it. The other options are ordinary descriptive statements that are true or false.

quiz.question: Gilbert Ryle's example of a visitor who tours Oxford's colleges and then asks where the University is illustrates which idea?
options: A language game
A felicity condition
A category mistake
A family resemblance
quiz.explanation: The visitor treats the University as one more building when it is the organisation of all of them; Ryle thought Descartes made the same mistake about the mind.

quiz.question: For the later Wittgenstein, the main task of philosophy is to dissolve confusions created by misunderstanding how language works, rather than to construct grand theories.
quiz.explanation: He described philosophy as a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by language, aiming to show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle.

quiz.question: A stranger in a supermarket says to a couple, “I now pronounce you married.” In Austin's terms, what has happened?
options: A successful locutionary act but no change in anyone's status
A felicitous performative creating a marriage
A false statement
A perlocutionary act of marrying
quiz.explanation: The words are uttered with meaning, but the performative misfires because the felicity conditions (the right person, procedure and circumstances) are not met. Performatives are infelicitous rather than false.

quiz.question: Which modern situation best illustrates the idea of meaning as use?
options: Looking up a word's etymology in a historical dictionary
A teenager learning what new slang means by hearing how friends use it in different situations
Memorising a list of chemical element names
Translating a word by pointing to a picture of it
quiz.explanation: Slang is learned by watching how a word functions across contexts, not from definitions or pictures. That is exactly Wittgenstein's model of understanding.

quiz.question: Ordinary language philosophy was criticised by Bertrand Russell and Ernest Gellner for making philosophy trivial and too deferential to everyday speech.
quiz.explanation: Russell disliked the later Wittgenstein's influence, and Gellner's *Words and Things* (1959) attacked the Oxford movement as conservative and trivial.

goDeeper.body:
The sharpest modern debate about the later Wittgenstein concerns **rule-following**. In section 201 of the *Investigations* he states a paradox: no course of action could be determined by a rule, because any course of action can be made out to accord with the rule. In 1982 Saul Kripke's *Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language* turned this into a startling sceptical argument. Suppose you have only ever added numbers smaller than 57. What fact about you, your past behaviour, your mental images, your dispositions, makes it true that by *plus* you meant addition rather than *quus*, a function that gives the same answers below 57 but gives 5 for anything larger? Kripke argued there is no such fact, and that Wittgenstein offered a sceptical solution: meaning-claims are justified by community agreement, not by inner facts. On this reading the private language argument is a corollary: a solitary individual has no community to check against.

Many specialists, such as G.P. Baker and P.M.S. Hacker, and John McDowell, protested that this is Kripkenstein, a hybrid creature. They point to the very next remarks, where Wittgenstein says there is a way of grasping a rule that is not an interpretation, but is shown in what we call obeying the rule and going against it in actual cases. On their reading the paradox is a reductio of the assumption that understanding must be an interpretation, not a sceptical discovery.

A second debate concerns whether Wittgenstein's quietism, his refusal to theorise, is coherent. Isn't “meaning is use” itself a theory? And can philosophy really leave everything as it is, as he claimed? Contemporary philosophers of language, from Robert Brandom's inferentialism to work on pragmatics descended from Austin and Paul Grice, have tried to turn his insights into systematic theory, which some would say betrays him.

readings.title: Philosophical Investigations
readings.author: Ludwig Wittgenstein
readings.note: Read sections 1–43 (language games and meaning as use) and 65–71 (family resemblance). The revised 4th edition, translated by Anscombe, Hacker and Schulte (2009), is excellent.

readings.title: Ludwig Wittgenstein: The Duty of Genius
readings.author: Ray Monk
readings.note: The definitive, gripping biography, which makes the connection between the man and the philosophy vivid.

readings.title: How to Do Things with Words
readings.author: J.L. Austin
readings.note: Short, witty lectures that founded speech act theory; the first three lectures are enough to get the idea.

readings.title: Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language
readings.author: Saul Kripke
readings.note: A brilliant, controversial reconstruction of the rule-following paradox; read it alongside a critic such as McDowell.

questions: If meaning is use, could a word's meaning change simply because people start using it differently? Is there anything wrong with that?
Is the family-resemblance view a refutation of Socrates' search for definitions, or just a refusal to play his game?
Can an AI system make a promise? Which of Austin's felicity conditions would it fail, if any?
